chunks: My father narrated to him, may God be pleased with him, who said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from al-Hasan Ali ibn Fadal, from Thalabah ibn Maymun, from some of our companions, from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What is the right of the believer upon the believer?

He said: There are seven obligatory rights, and there is no right among them except that it is obligatory upon him; and if he opposes it, he leaves the guardianship of God and abandons His obedience, and God Almighty has no share in him. I said: May I be your ransom, tell me what they are?

He said: Woe to you, O Mu'alla! I am affectionate towards you; I fear that you will be lost and not retain, and know but not act. I said: There is no power except with God. He said: The easiest of them is that you love for him what you love for yourself, and dislike for him what you dislike for yourself.

The second right is that you walk in his neighborhood and seek his pleasure and do not contradict his word, and the third right is that you connect to him with your self, your wealth, your hand, your foot, and your tongue.

The fourth right is that you be his eye, his guide, his mirror, and his garment. The fifth right is that you are not full while he is hungry, and you are clothed while he is naked, and you are satisfied (with water) while he is thirsty.
ai.seo_question: What are the seven rights of a believer upon another believer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Khisal*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) defines the comprehensive bond of *wilayah* through seven rights, emphasizing that mutual love and practical service are essential for maintaining divine connection. This framework extends beyond spiritual affinity to include tangible acts of generosity, such as sharing resources and personal assistance, reflecting the Shia concept of *ta'awun* (cooperation) in righteousness. The narration underscores that fulfilling these rights ensures one's inclusion in God's sphere of authority, linking interpersonal ethics directly to theological standing.
